item.dc:creator: Marco Rubio, Secretary of State
item.description:
Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

Niue National Day

Press Statement

October 18, 2026

On behalf of the United States of America, I extend my warmest congratulations to the people of Niue as you celebrate the 52nd anniversary of your self-governance.

This year marked an important milestone in the partnership between our two countries as we named the first U.S. Ambassador to Niue. This historic milestone builds on the diplomatic relationship our countries established in 2023 and America’s commitment to deepening ties with the people of Niue.

We value our work together advancing regional unity and security through the Pacific Islands Forum, where the Deputy Secretary recently announced U.S. support to address the ongoing global energy crisis and to combat illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing in the region.

I look forward to expanding our cooperation in the years to come and send my best wishes to all Niueans on your Constitution Day.

Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

Joint Base Andrews

Secretary of State Marco Rubio Remarks to the Press

Remarks

October 17, 2026

QUESTION:  Mr. Secretary?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  What’s going on?

QUESTION:  Nice and chilly, right? 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  It’s all right. 

QUESTION:  With everything going on in the world and with crisis all over, why are you choosing now, at this time, to go to Uzbekistan?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, it’s the time of year that worked for those leaders.  It’s not just Uzbekistan, it’s the other four countries from Central Asia.  This is an important relationship.  I mean, one of the things that suffers is the strategic business.  You’re always visiting someplace where there’s a crisis or there’s a problem or there’s a – you’re going because there’s a conference.  But there’s countries you’d like to get to because we want to build our relationships with them.  And so that’s what we did a couple weeks ago when we went to Greece and other places like that, and earlier, a few weeks earlier than that, we went to Latin America, and now to Central Asia.  So – and the chance to see – it was the date that worked to get all five of the leaders together, all five of the foreign ministers from the five countries. 

QUESTION:  On Starshield, what’s going on?  Because Elon Musk said it’s up to the President. 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, Starshield or Starlink?

QUESTION:  Well, just both. 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah, I know, it’s confusing.  So Starlink is a commercial product, okay?  And so they – it’s regulated and handled as a commercial product.  Starshield is a defense product, a military product.  And as I said, I mean, that is something that we have a military – the United States military uses.  It’s not at this moment available to Ukraine, and that’s under conversation.  It’s under discussion right now of how they would want to use it. 

QUESTION:  No, but did the U.S. – did the U.S. have anything to do with it not working in Ukraine?  Zelenskyy said it was deliberate.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  No.  Well, I don’t know what Zelenskyy said.  I’m not sure Zelenskyy knows what he’s talking about, but it wasn’t deliberate.  We have nothing to do with that.  I don’t – the United States, nobody ordered that Starlink speed to be slowed down.  It sort of happened, but my understanding is it’s been restored.  It’s back to where it was before.  That’s Starlink, though.  They were using Starlink for their drones. 

QUESTION:  Has Starshield been restored? 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Starshield is a totally different product.  Starshield is –

QUESTION:  I know, but is it –

SECRETARY RUBIO:  No, no, Starshield is a contract with the U.S. military.  It has nothing to do with Ukraine.  I know Ukraine wants access to Starshield.  They do not have Starshield now.  They’ve asked for access to it in order to conduct deep strikes inside of Russia.  They do not have access to it at this moment.  Those are two different products. 

QUESTION:  But you have to have a theory as to why, obviously, Ukraine has reported disruptions.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah, I don’t know what their theory is, but nothing to do with the White House.  I saw a report on that the other day.  It’s just categorically false.  No one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet or slow down speed so that certain drones couldn’t use it.  But my understanding is it’s back up and running.  That’s what I read – that’s what we heard two days ago.

QUESTION:  Sir, on the sanctions waivers on Russia.  Senator Ted Cruz today called it a big mistake that only serves to benefit Putin.  I’m wondering what your response is to that. 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, there are other countries – the problem is these sanctions were not just sanctions on Russia.  They include tariffs on a number of countries – India, for example, and others.  And so I think the President wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyze what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the U.S. economy.  I think when the bill was passed, one of the reasons the waivers were put in there is understanding that they would need some period of time to study this, given all the different things that are going on in the world right now, including the pressure on global energy supplies that are happening not just because of Iran, not just because of the Straits of Hormuz, but increasingly because of the Houthis attacking Saudi Arabia and because of the war with Ukraine and Russia, where energy infrastructure is being hit.  And so that’s having an impact on global prices as well.

So, I think you have to take all of that into account and weigh it against each other.  And then you’ve got countries like India, for example, that have voluntarily diversified their energy portfolio but are still getting a substantial amount of energy from Russia because it’s hard to pivot from one day to the next, but they’re also an important ally and partner of the United States.  So, the President – we need that period of time to sort of study all this and figure out what the right combination is.

QUESTION:  Between this waiver and the diesel deal, I mean, there’s a criticism that you’re basically giving Putin something for nothing, we’re giving Putin these freebies.  What’s your response?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, that diesel was going to be sold one way or the other.  I mean, the diesel that Putin is going to sell, they would make it available to the global market one way or the other.  The only difference is how much of it the United States was going to get.  So – but this is not unprecedented.  If you recall a few months ago, we also did a 60-day waiver on Russian oil when Hormuz was being challenged. 

So yeah, these conflicts around the world are starting to crash into each other, and they’re having an impact not just on global oil and diesel prices, but on economics.  And I mean, the United States, we’re paying higher prices than we all want to be paying, but you look at some of these other countries around the world, they’re near crisis mode.  So, all of these things have to be managed delicately and worked with because they’re all – they’re all coming together now.  It’s not just the Strait of Hormuz anymore.  It’s what’s happening with Saudi Arabia and the uncertainty that that’s creating.  It’s also what’s happening between Russia and Ukraine and the constraints that’s putting on global energy supplies.

QUESTION:  I’d like to ask you about violence in the West Bank.  My colleague, Heidi Levine, was attacked there yesterday. 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  I saw that.  We’re all – we’re very disturbed by those images and what we’re seeing.  We’ve asked the Israelis and continue to ask them to crack down on that stuff.  That – the President’s been very clear.  He’s said this repeatedly.  He does not want to see friction or anything, a crisis, going on in the West Bank.  Now, I understand that these are groups that are out there doing it, and the President has been repeatedly clear when he’s said that he doesn’t want to see that.  He doesn’t want to see a new spark. 

But we saw the reports about what happened yesterday.  I don’t have all the details.  I only go off media reports.  I know we’ve inquired with the embassy, are supposed to get a cable back later today or tomorrow indicating exactly what they know about it.  But from what I understand about media reports, it didn’t look good.  It was an American reporter; there was a photo of a journalist who was caught behind where some of these groups came in and was beaten.  There’s video of that.  So look, the whole thing was just disturbing and didn’t – not a good look. 

QUESTION:  Mr. Secretary, the President, one of the first decisions he took was to lift sanctions against the settlers.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah, I understand, but he doesn’t want to see what’s happening now. 

QUESTION:  No, that’s not –

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Lifting sanctions, which he did earlier in the day, does not mean he’s a supporter of what he’s seeing now on television, what he’s reading about.  We’d like to get all the facts and learn a little bit more about it, but that – look, that’s one instance, and it happened to involve a photojournalist.  But there are other instances we’ve had complaints about.  Now it’s this olive harvest season, and so traditionally that’s always been a time in which a lot of people come into those areas.  So, we’ve been watching that closely.  We know that’s an issue there, that’s potentially an issue in Lebanon as well.  Okay?

QUESTION:  Do you agree with the UK assessment, the intel assessment that Russia and Iran may be increasing hybrid attacks over the next few months? 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  But which assessment are you talking about? 

QUESTION:  The – both NATO and UK have indicated –

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Oh, NATO.

QUESTION:  Have indicated that in –

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah, but those are two separate things.  So in the case of – you’re asking about Russian hybrid attacks.  Yeah, we’ve always been concerned that the war in Ukraine can metastasize into other parts of Europe and other parts of the world, whether it be sabotage operations or the like.  We’ve always been concerned that that’s one of the risks of a stalemated conflict, is escalation, and escalation can take the form of irregular attacks or irregular events.  So that’s something I raised a couple weeks ago and we’re watching that closely. 

I think with Iran and UK, what the UK has said is that the Iranians were behind the plot to attack the air base.  And obviously we have no reason to disagree with the assessment factually.  In fact, we agree with it.

So, all right?  It’s cold, guys.

QUESTION:  On the case regarding my colleague, what’s –

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Did you guys see my Gators today take down Texas on the road?  

Go ahead. 

QUESTION:  The case regarding my colleague who was attacked in the West Bank, what steps will you take to ensure that there’s a proper investigation of this incident? 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, we want to learn all the facts about it first.  Obviously, we’ve seen the video, and we’ve seen the media reporting about it.  We have a process to handle these sorts of things.  And if, in fact, it turns out to be what it appears it was, then we have ways of communicating that to the Israelis about how we expect – that we would expect them to prevent that from happening in the future.  And it’s – again, the President doesn’t want to see a crisis in the West Bank.  We don’t need that right now.  Israel doesn’t need that right now. 

QUESTION:  Can I ask briefly on Eritrea-Ethiopia?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah. 

QUESTION:  How high-risk is the chance of war between them?  And do you feel like it was a mistake to lift some of those Ethiopia-related sanctions right before violence flared up? 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  No, I don’t think those – I don’t – no, I don’t think the sanctions lifting – these were very small sanctions, and they don’t really have anything to do with what’s happening over there.  You have these separatists that were attacking inside of Ethiopia.  You had an Ethiopian response to it.  You see troops surging on both sides of the border as a result of that.  And anytime you see troops on both sides of the border in a place like that, you’re always worried that that can turn into a broader conflict.

So, we don’t have the closest relationship with Eritrea, obviously, over the years, although we’ve had communication with them – more than usual – in the past few months.  Our hope was that by lifting some of these sanctions, we can increase those links because it’s hard to serve the role of mediator and peacemaker unless you can talk to both sides.

Obviously, the Ethiopian side we talk to a lot more, and I spoke to them this week personally, a few days ago, and just reiterated how important it was – like, we understand the challenge you’re facing from these separatists, and obviously no one is supportive of terrorism and the terrorist attacks that came against them – drone attacks against their own capital – but we also think we – it’s a time to sort of be wise and measured in how you respond to that and make sure it doesn’t turn into a broader war which could ultimately pull in other countries.  The last thing the world needs right now is another war.

Okay?  Thank you, guys.

Office of the Spokesman

United States Hosts Caribbean Dialogue to Advance Shared Security and Prosperity

Media Note

October 16, 2026

On October 15, Deputy Secretary of State Landau hosted the U.S.-Caribbean Dialogue at the Department of State, delivering on the commitment Secretary Rubio made to Caribbean Community (CARICOM) Heads of Government at their February meeting in Saint Kitts and Nevis.  High-level delegations from Antigua and Barbuda, The Bahamas, Barbados, Belize, Dominica, the Dominican Republic, Grenada, Guyana, Haiti, Jamaica, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, Suriname, and Trinidad and Tobago joined the United States to expand cooperation on shared economic, energy, and security priorities.  At a business luncheon and an evening reception, Caribbean delegations met with American business leaders to discuss opportunities for projects in energy, critical minerals, ports, and digital infrastructure that will create jobs and growth in both the United States and the Caribbean.

Dialogue sessions addressed energy security, economic growth, critical infrastructure, trusted technology, disaster response and health cooperation, and the fight against narco-terrorists and transnational criminal organizations.  Participants discussed access to U.S. energy and technology, fair and transparent procurement, trusted digital and port infrastructure, self-sufficient health workforces, and closer coordination to disrupt illicit narcotics and firearms trafficking.

Advancing U.S.-Caribbean Commercial Diplomacy

  • Caribbean Investment Summit: The Department of State announced that it will host a Caribbean Investment Summit in early 2027 to connect U.S. companies, financiers, and government finance agencies with Caribbean partners to help them close deals in open, competitive markets.

Promoting Trusted Digital Technology

  • Caribbean and Central America Undersea Cables Program: The Department of State announced $175.8 million to expand trusted, high-speed undersea cable connectivity across the Caribbean and Central America and make trusted connections more resilient to disruption.

Strengthening Health Self-Sufficiency

  • Americas Strategic Partnership for Independent Regional Healthcare Excellence (ASPIRE): Working with Congress, the Department of State intends to provide $61.5 million through ASPIRE to help Caribbean governments build self-sufficient health workforces by hiring health professionals ethically and transparently, with fair pay going to the workers themselves.

Advancing Regional Security Through the Caribbean Basin Security Initiative (CBSI)

  • Protecting Critical Infrastructure and Maritime Resources: The Department of State announced $37 million in CBSI programming to secure critical digital infrastructure and ports, and counter illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing.

United States Hosts Caribbean Dialogue to Advance Shared Security and Prosperity

Media Note

October 16, 2026

On October 15, Deputy Secretary of State Landau hosted the U.S.-Caribbean Dialogue at the Department of State, delivering on the commitment Secretary Rubio made to Caribbean Community (CARICOM) Heads of Government at their February meeting in Saint Kitts and Nevis.  High-level delegations from Antigua and Barbuda, The Bahamas, Barbados, Belize, Dominica, the Dominican Republic, Grenada, Guyana, Haiti, Jamaica, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, Suriname, and Trinidad and Tobago joined the United States to expand cooperation on shared economic, energy, and security priorities.  At a business luncheon and an evening reception, Caribbean delegations met with American business leaders to discuss opportunities for projects in energy, critical minerals, ports, and digital infrastructure that will create jobs and growth in both the United States and the Caribbean.

Dialogue sessions addressed energy security, economic growth, critical infrastructure, trusted technology, disaster response and health cooperation, and the fight against narco-terrorists and transnational criminal organizations.  Participants discussed access to U.S. energy and technology, fair and transparent procurement, trusted digital and port infrastructure, self-sufficient health workforces, and closer coordination to disrupt illicit narcotics and firearms trafficking.

Advancing U.S.-Caribbean Commercial Diplomacy

  • Caribbean Investment Summit: The Department of State announced that it will host a Caribbean Investment Summit in early 2027 to connect U.S. companies, financiers, and government finance agencies with Caribbean partners to help them close deals in open, competitive markets.

Office of the Spokesman

State Department Announces Feed the Future Innovation Labs to Support Agriculture Research

Media Note

October 15, 2026

Today, the State Department announced eight Feed the Future Innovation Labs in partnership with U.S. Land Grant Universities from around the country.  The Labs put American researchers to work on global threats to agriculture that do not stop at the border, such as crop pests, livestock disease, and depleted soils before they reach U.S. farms and grocery shelves, delivering direct returns for American taxpayers.  Research on animal health, cereals, and soil fertility helps protect U.S. producers from emerging threats.  Work on coffee, cacao, and peanuts strengthens the supply chains behind products Americans buy every day.  Helping developing countries become more productive builds future markets for American firms, farmers, trade organizations, and research organizations.

The track record is proven. Investment in U.S. university-led international agricultural research returns $8 for every $1 invested.  This helps keep American universities at the forefront of agricultural science and trains the next generation of researchers across the United States.

The universities and their respective Innovation Labs include:  

  • Auburn University: Feed the Future Innovation Lab for Fertilizer and Soil Health
  • University of Florida: Feed the Future Innovation Lab for High Value Crops – Safeguarding Agriculture, Food, and Economy (SAFE)
  • University of Georgia: Feed the Future Food Innovation Lab for Peanut
  • University of Hawaii: Feed the Future Innovation Lab for Coffee and Cacao
  • Kansas State University: Feed the Future Innovation Lab for Cereals and Feed the Future Innovation Lab for Sustainable Intensification of Targeted Agricultural Systems (SITAS)
  • Mississippi State University: Feed the Future Innovation Lab for Fish
  • Washington State University: Feed the Future Innovation Lab for Animal Health

item.title: Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau With Saint Lucia Prime Minister and CARICOM Chair Philip J. Pierre at the Opening Remarks of the U.S.-Caribbean Dialogue
item.dc:creator: Christopher Landau, Deputy Secretary of State, Philip J. Pierre, Saint Lucia Prime Minister, Susan Walke, State Department Director for Caribbean Affairs , Juan Pablo Segura, Assistant Secretary for Western Hemisphere Affairs
item.description:
Christopher Landau, Deputy Secretary of State

Philip J. Pierre, Saint Lucia Prime Minister

Susan Walke, State Department Director for Caribbean Affairs

Juan Pablo Segura, Assistant Secretary for Western Hemisphere Affairs

Washington, DC

Loy Henderson Conference Room

Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau With Saint Lucia Prime Minister and CARICOM Chair Philip J. Pierre at the Opening Remarks of the U.S.-Caribbean Dialogue

Remarks

October 15, 2026

MS WALKE:  Good morning, everyone, and welcome.  My name is Susan Walke I’m the director for Caribbean affairs here at the State Department, and I will be your emcee for today’s dialogue.  We are looking forward to a day of in-depth discussions on a number of key issues of importance to all of our countries. 

I am delighted to introduce you to Assistant Secretary for Western Hemisphere Affairs, Juan Pablo Segura.  Assistant Secretary Segura was sworn in as assistant secretary of state on August 14th.  Before joining the State Department, he was the secretary of commerce and trade for the Commonwealth of Virginia for Governor Glenn Youngkin.  As secretary, he was responsible for growing Virginia’s more than $710 billion a year in GDP economy, and managed the state’s international trade portfolio.  Assistant Secretary Segura, I’m pleased to welcome you up to the dais.  (Applause.)  

ASSISTANT SECRETARY SEGURA:  Thank you, Susan, for that great introduction.  It’s a true honor to be here with all of you this morning, this incredible group of distinguished leaders across the Caribbean.   

I’d like to start with just a reminder that Secretary Rubio made a promise earlier this year at Saint Kitts and Nevis.  He promised that the U.S. would step up in the Caribbean, and this is a manifestation of that promise.  This dialogue is the U.S. making good on its promise, which is incredibly exciting for all of us at the United States.  

As you review the agenda, as we have the conversation that – the conversations that will happen over the next two years, you’ll see that the agenda mirrors the objectives of the Bureau of Western Hemisphere Affairs.  Our objectives are very simple.  The first is we want to uplift the region through economic investment.  The second is we want to end the scourge of narcoterrorist threat across the hemisphere.  And the third is we want to end illegal immigration.  We want countries to have sovereignty, true sovereignty, across the hemisphere.  

Now, as I introduce my boss, Deputy Secretary Landau, I do want to just highlight that this conversation really touches the why of why this conversation is so important.  And I was recently speaking to one of you a week ago or a week and a half ago at the OAS, and it was very encouraging to see how everyone was leaning into the dialogue with the United States, but there was also a part of conversation where folks didn’t know the tools that are available in this economic conversation, this security conversation.  A lot of folks don’t know that the President has prioritized 20 percent of our foreign assistance to the hemisphere.  A lot of people don’t know that the DFC, the Development Finance Corporation, the mandate has changed.   

The tools, the investment opportunities have changed.  The (inaudible) has changed in how we can help countries grow economically and so I feel like there’s no better person to be the keynote speaker for today than the chair of the board of the DFC, a former ambassador, someone that knows the conversations, the real conversations that are happening at posts with your countries.  And so it is an honor for me to introduce our incredible deputy secretary of state for the United States of America, Deputy Secretary Landau.  (Applause.) 

DEPUTY SECRETARY LANDAU:  Thank you, Assistant Secretary.  Welcome to our friends from the Caribbean.  It’s really a pleasure to have such a distinguished group of leaders here today.  I think this kind of dialogue is, frankly, overdue.  

And I want to just start with what to me is the central reality underlying all of this, which is the United States is a Caribbean nation.  You all know that.  That is true as a matter of geography.  We have – Puerto Rico is in the Caribbean.  It’s true of our history.  I was just discussing with several of you how Alexander Hamilton is from Nevis and, frankly, a huge part of our economy was the triangular trade between Europe, the eastern shore of the United States, the Caribbean.  The relationships between the United States and this part of the world have been crucial throughout our history and throughout your history.  And so we’re not writing on a blank slate as we gather here.   

I think you all know this far better than I do, that the ties between our countries are not only historical; they involve people.  When I was in Antigua last year, I was talking to somebody and I think of his siblings, two of them were in the States, and the cousins were in the States.  The personal bonds between our countries are amazing.  So many successful people in the United States, in this generation and previous generations, have come from your region.  I’m going all the way back to Alexander Hamilton, but people like Colin Powell, who ran this building 25 years ago.  I mean, our country has benefitted enormously from the ties with your region.   

And frankly, it has been a source of pain for many of us as Americans to see the United States not giving the Western Hemisphere generally the attention it deserved, and specifically the Caribbean.  The Caribbean is very much part of the Western Hemisphere.  So I’m sure you’ve all seen the stories about how the United States is, under President Trump and Secretary Rubio – we are making the Western Hemisphere a – we’re not – we are restoring – I think that’s the better word – the Western Hemisphere to its position of preeminence and priority in American foreign policy.  For far too long, we have been looking at things that are happening halfway across the world, and we have been ignoring things that are happening right in our own neighborhood.  

And so I just want to – I think it’s very important that we recognize some of the flaws of recent years in our policies and we talk together to commit to ways that we can build institutional relationships.  Because all of us in this room – I mean, we all have government positions, and it’s great, it lasts for a while.  But then all of us will be gone in a matter of years, right?  And I think the challenge for us is to create a lasting foundation that doesn’t just depend on so-and-so being friends with so-and-so.  I mean, it’s wonderful and it’s great.  One of the great things about these kinds of gatherings is that we can establish personal relationships, right?  It’s great if I can have you on WhatsApp or that kind of thing.  But that is not the basis for a lasting institutional structure of a relationship that’s going to survive over decades.   

And I think – that’s what I’m hoping that a conference like today can establish – really both those things.  I mean, again, personal ties are important in diplomacy.  But again, I think I’m looking to strengthen the structural ties, again, many of which are there.  I mean, we’re not building this from scratch, and I think we have a lot of historical precedent.  But I also want to make clear that we in the United States do not have all the answers, right?  I think I entered this job with a fair dose of humility that – I grew up in Latin America myself.  My father was a diplomat and – including in Venezuela, where actually when – during the years in the early 80s when he lived in – when we lived in Venezuela, I actually had the opportunity to visit many of your countries for the first time.  That’s when I first got the chance to go to Haiti, to Barbados, to Grenada, way back more than 40 years ago now.  And again, that only underscored for me obviously the great diversity in the Caribbean but also the importance in so many areas of the United States with these relationships in the Caribbean. 

So bringing together the leaders has been a real – your leaders – all of you has been something that’s been very important both for Secretary Rubio and for me.  I think he was delighted to go to CARICOM.  I think it was in – was it in Saint Nevis or in Saint Kitts and Nevis?  He was at a meeting or – he went recently.  And so I think he very much – again, as somebody from Florida – understands better than anybody the importance of this Caribbean region to the United States, across all dynamics, again, on a human level, on a economic level, on a security level.   

And so, again, I just want to underscore that I think this dialogue is overdue, and I just want to underscore that – I want to underscore the word “dialogue,” right?  A dialogue doesn’t mean that you have come here to have me or anybody else in the United States just give lectures, right?  I mean, I just think it’s very important that we, the United States, listen to you from the Caribbean what your vision is.  I mean, you obviously are – you all are sovereign countries; you are going to decide your fate.  And – but I think – honestly, I truly believe we wouldn’t be having this meeting if the Secretary and I didn’t believe that what is in your interests is also in our interests; that there are many, many areas where we should be deepening cooperation where there are great solutions. 

So again, I will talk today in part about further commitments the United States is going to make, and that’s fine.  I was reading through the remarks that they prepared for me here; it’s like, well, we’ll give millions of dollars for this and millions of dollars for that.  Ultimately, I’m more interested – and I think you should be more interested, or I would hope that you would be more interested – in, like, where do we get the businesses that are going to be there for the long term, that are investing in real economic opportunities that are creating a lasting foundation for the relationships?  Because ultimately, a particular grant can be fine to fill a particular need, but for a long-term growth strategy, a particular grant isn’t going to fix that.  Now, there may be particular grants that are useful insofar as they create a framework or a foundation for private-sector-led economic development.  But ultimately, I think that’s what’s going to, frankly, be the main driver here. 

So again, I just was talking to the representative of Suriname before we walked in here, and they said they had a great meeting, I think yesterday, with a private American security company that offered some services that could help them really improve their own security for their country.  I said to me, that is great.  And I feel my job, our job here at the Department of State, is to be the connective tissue between you, the leaders from your region, and the dynamic American private sector.  The American private sector is going to have more creative, cost-effective solutions for the problems you’re looking at than the U.S. Government will.  I’ll just tell you that.  I say that as somebody who works for the government right now.   

But ultimately, the greatness of the United States is not driven by the government; it’s driven by our private sector.  And so our job – or what I see our job as being is just to be an interlocutor so that our private sector is aware of the opportunities in the Caribbean, and that the Caribbean is aware of what the private sector might be interested in here.  I mean, it’s a conversation that has to go both ways. 

So let’s actually start talking a little bit about economics.  One of the things that makes me very happy is that we’re launching an investment dialogue next year precisely to bring together all of your countries with the American private sector.  And so I think – this is an issue that I also fostered out in the Pacific region.  That’s another area I’ve been very focused on, some of the island states, some of which have some similarities to some of the islands – nations of the Caribbean – not that big in terms of land mass of the country or even the population.  So they present kind of interesting economic models, where there can be opportunities for economic development, but it’s not necessarily the most obvious target as a mass export market for American companies, let’s say, but where there might be investment opportunities that you all are interested in.   

But I think for this kind of an investment conference to work, it needs a lot of advanced thought from both sides.  I think I really would urge all of your countries to think about what kind of American private sector investment you are particularly interested in in your country.  If you have an infrastructure project, a port, or a digital infrastructure project, an energy infrastructure project that you’re interested in; you want to talk to people in the telecommunications area – I mean, if you all – again, it’d be most helpful if you all let us know in advance.  If you want to see a specific company, you say, I would like to see Google, I would like to see Bechtel, I would like to see a shipping company, I’d like to see American Airlines – whatever it is, that will make this kind of a conference more helpful.  Because we don’t want to just have a conference for the sake of bringing people together to meet; we want to actually be able to have people who are actually interested in pursuing deals.  And again, we will also reach out to the private sector and say, who is interested in opportunities in the Caribbean?  And again, we will try to work it both ways. 

But again, I encourage you to really give some thought.  I don’t really have the details about what month this is yet next year, but I know it is next year.  We will keep in touch on that.  Again, that just makes me very, very happy, because ultimately, again, it’s this kind of investments that will create growth and jobs in your country and build skills. 

We also recognize that economic development entails health.  And we understand some of the health needs in your region.   

And on health, this is when I start – this is what – I’m starting to tell some of the goodies that I’m here to talk about.  I’m happy to announce we have 61 – set aside $61.5 million to launch ASPIRE, the America Strategic Partnership for Independent Regional Healthcare Excellence – that’s a long one – in order to allow the region to build its own strong, self-reliant health care workforce capacity.  So again, I think we can get more details on that, but that’s one of the deliverables that I wanted to announce to you all today.   

Second, I wanted to talk a little bit about security, and I think the assistant secretary alluded to this.  I think we have seen an uptick in recent years of drugs coming through the Caribbean from South America towards the United States.  I don’t need to tell you what a danger this is for all of us.  And frankly, as you’ve all seen if you read the news, the United States is not going to just sit by with business as usual where we have more than 100,000 Americans dying of overdose from some of these drugs just in perpetuity.  I think we’re – we have followed a approach of using the judicial system, asking for arrests, extraditions, trying people.  And I think, as you’ve seen, we now recognize that this is actually also a national security threat to our people.  We’re taking actions accordingly.  And we’d like to work with your countries to make sure that we’re all on the same page, at least in recognizing the common danger of this and seeing how we can try to address this scourge together.   

So we already have a Caribbean Basin Security Initiative, and that’s the foundation of our security partnership with 13 of the countries.  And today we are – again, my next deliverable that I’m announcing is that we’re increasing our support through CBSI, and I’m pleased to announce $37 million in new programming to protect critical digital infrastructure and strengthen port security.  Obviously, strong ports are the first line of defense.  If drugs are coming into your ports – or it’s not just drugs also; it’s also weapons and other illegal goods.  I mean, and I think in my first week in the job, the Secretary called me down to his office and handed me an article about guns going to Haiti from the Miami River and said, “Could you please deal with this?”  And that was the beginning of what has been a pretty intense involvement, as the prime minister of Haiti here, my friend, Prime Minister Fils-Aimé, knows.  I’ve been very involved in Haiti, but it really stemmed out of trying to stop the flow of guns that are going from our country into Haiti and destabilizing it.   

And I will say on this note, I am working closely with our U.S. attorney in the Southern District of Florida to make sure that our law enforcement capabilities are fully mobilized and that we are coordinating with them, so if there are issues where you think the American judicial system can actually be helpful to you as leaders in your countries who are trying to solve particular problems – if there are criminal networks that are exporting drugs from your country and you think your country may not have all the infrastructure or the legal infrastructure to address this problem, let’s work together on some of these security challenges, because our U.S. Attorney’s Office in Miami is very eager to work with you on that.   

Another big priority is illegal fishing, and I’d like to – that’s been a priority of mine worldwide.  If there are people fishing illegally in your waters, we want to work with you to address that, because obviously fish is a important resource for all of our peoples.  And I’m also – on this issue, I’m announcing an additional $55.5 million to strengthen law enforcement – I told you I had a lot of millions here to talk about – 55.5 million to strengthen law enforcement and $11 million in Foreign Military Financing to build the capabilities of your security forces.  So again, I think let’s talk about how we can work together with the security ministers, with CARICOM IMPACS, to convene the next Caribbean Basin Security Initiative security ministerial in spring 2027, next spring.   

Third – and I see I’m running low on time, but I just want to cover a range of issues that – I’m sure that all of you can flesh out what’s on your mind – trusted infrastructure is really important, and particularly secure communications networks.  Ultimately, a modern economy cannot exist without a secure network.  We all have seen vulnerabilities.  Every day you read about it in the news.  And – but without a good digital footprint, you can’t have a solid banking system, tourism system, energy grid, or government services.  And who builds those networks matters, and we would like to work with you on that.  In fact, on this – in this connection, I’m announcing $175.8 million in U.S. investment in secure infrastructure through our Caribbean and Central America underseas cables program.  This will provide trusted, high-speed connectivity across the region to build resilient, secure networks that serve your people and not outside interests.   

So together, the numbers that I have mentioned really total hundreds of millions of dollars in new commitments, but it’s not just about a certain dollar amount.  It’s about just the long term, the United States reaffirming its interest and commitment to this critical region.   

So I just want to end by underscoring the values that I think that we all share: respect for national sovereignty, the rule of law, open markets.  These are some of the central tenets that underlie our relationships.  And these are – by focusing on these core issues, that’s how we’re going to stimulate economic growth, attract investment, and allow you and us to provide prosperity and security for our – your citizens and our citizens.  So again, as somebody who is very, very committed to your region, I just say that there are few events that I have attended during my time as Deputy Secretary of State that I’m as excited to be part of as this one.   

I will close by just saying my last class in college, at Harvard College, was Sociology 113 that was taught by Orlando Patterson.  He was visiting at Harvard that year.  And it was on the sociology of the Caribbean, just all the many fascinating aspects of culture that emerged in your region.  I mean, you have such an interesting mixture, just looking at the backgrounds of your countries.  And I remember my last exam in college was comparing Rastafarianism in Jamaica with Vodou in Haiti and how some of those ancestral beliefs affected the modern development of those countries. 

And I just want to say that, at least in me, I want you to know that you have a true friend of the Caribbean, someone who, again, is very cognizant of the critical role that your region has always played in the development of our country, and I think it is – you’re part of our past, you’re part of our present, and part of our future, and vice versa, I think.  And I just want to, on that note, say how pleased and excited I am to welcome all of you here.  And I hope this is a very enriching experience for all of you, as I’m sure it will be for us.  Thank you very much.  (Applause.) 

MS WALKE:  Thank you.  And may I now ask Prime Minister Pierre of Saint Lucia, our CARICOM chair, to please come to the podium to deliver your remarks?  Thank you.  (Applause.)   

PRIME MINISTER PIERRE:  Thank you very much.  Good morning, everyone.  Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau, Assistant Secretary Juan Pablo, fellow heads of government, heads of delegation, ladies and gentlemen, I’ve been told I have three minutes.  (Laughter.) 

DEPUTY SECRETARY LANDAU:  I’m sorry.  I went way over on mine, so —  

PRIME MINISTER PIERRE:  I shall remain within my three minutes.  Good morning, everyone.  I speak as Prime Minister of Saint Lucia and chairman of the Caribbean Community.  I thank the Government of the United States for convening this dialogue and for its hospitality.  This meeting responds to the call by CARICOM leaders for political-level consultations following our constructive engagement with Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Saint Kitts and Nevis in February.   

We value this relationship.  Our countries are connected by geography, commerce, tourism, family, and friendship.  The Caribbean community is a close neighbor, a stable democratic partner, and a region open to investment.  We seek a more strategic partnership sustained by regular dialogue and measured by improvements in the daily lives of our people.   

For Caribbean families, energy security means affordable electricity.  Economic cooperation means jobs, investment, and opportunity.  Security cooperation means safer communities.  Disaster preparedness means knowing that help will arrive when it is needed and will arrive promptly.  These are shared interests. 

Our discussions today should translate into practical commitments financing for resilient energy systems, predictable trade and stronger commercial partnerships, secure infrastructure, stronger health systems and disaster response, and coordinated action against organized crime and illicit firearms trafficking.  Haiti must remain central to our attention.  We appreciate the U.S.’s role and welcome the extension of the United Nations mandate for the Gang Suppression Force.  CARICOM continues – continues its work through the Eminent Persons Group.  Sustained international assistance and credible elections with the widest possible participation are essential to restoring confidence and supporting Haiti’s return to stability. 

Our dialogue must also make room for immigration and migration matters, with profound implications for our communities and our people-to-people ties.  The strength of today’s meeting will be demonstrated by what follows it.  Let us connect political dialogue with sustained technical engagements, identify priorities, and establish clear arrangements for follow-up between governments and the private sector.  The CARICOM Secretariat will help coordinate the community’s technical work alongside our national authorities and regional institutions.  CARICOM comes to this table ready to listen, ready to engage, and ready to build a partnership that delivers mutual benefit, with respect for our sovereignty and our shared aspirations. 

I look forward to these discussions and the (inaudible) development of the people of the region.  I thank you.  (Applause.)

October 15, 2026

I am delighted to introduce you to Assistant Secretary for Western Hemisphere Affairs, Juan Pablo Segura.  Assistant Secretary Segura was sworn in as assistant secretary of state on August 14th.  Before joining the State Department, he was the secretary of commerce and trade for the Commonwealth of Virginia for Governor Glenn Youngkin.  As secretary, he was responsible for growing Virginia’s more than $710 billion a year in GDP economy, and managed the state’s international trade portfolio.  Assistant Secretary Segura, I’m pleased to welcome you up to the dais.  (Applause.)  

ASSISTANT SECRETARY SEGURA:  Thank you, Susan, for that great introduction.  It’s a true honor to be here with all of you this morning, this incredible group of distinguished leaders across the Caribbean.   

I’d like to start with just a reminder that Secretary Rubio made a promise earlier this year at Saint Kitts and Nevis.  He promised that the U.S. would step up in the Caribbean, and this is a manifestation of that promise.  This dialogue is the U.S. making good on its promise, which is incredibly exciting for all of us at the United States.  

As you review the agenda, as we have the conversation that – the conversations that will happen over the next two years, you’ll see that the agenda mirrors the objectives of the Bureau of Western Hemisphere Affairs.  Our objectives are very simple.  The first is we want to uplift the region through economic investment.  The second is we want to end the scourge of narcoterrorist threat across the hemisphere.  And the third is we want to end illegal immigration.  We want countries to have sovereignty, true sovereignty, across the hemisphere.  

Now, as I introduce my boss, Deputy Secretary Landau, I do want to just highlight that this conversation really touches the why of why this conversation is so important.  And I was recently speaking to one of you a week ago or a week and a half ago at the OAS, and it was very encouraging to see how everyone was leaning into the dialogue with the United States, but there was also a part of conversation where folks didn’t know the tools that are available in this economic conversation, this security conversation.  A lot of folks don’t know that the President has prioritized 20 percent of our foreign assistance to the hemisphere.  A lot of people don’t know that the DFC, the Development Finance Corporation, the mandate has changed.   

The tools, the investment opportunities have changed.  The (inaudible) has changed in how we can help countries grow economically and so I feel like there’s no better person to be the keynote speaker for today than the chair of the board of the DFC, a former ambassador, someone that knows the conversations, the real conversations that are happening at posts with your countries.  And so it is an honor for me to introduce our incredible deputy secretary of state for the United States of America, Deputy Secretary Landau.  (Applause.) 

DEPUTY SECRETARY LANDAU:  Thank you, Assistant Secretary.  Welcome to our friends from the Caribbean.  It’s really a pleasure to have such a distinguished group of leaders here today.  I think this kind of dialogue is, frankly, overdue.  

And I want to just start with what to me is the central reality underlying all of this, which is the United States is a Caribbean nation.  You all know that.  That is true as a matter of geography.  We have – Puerto Rico is in the Caribbean.  It’s true of our history.  I was just discussing with several of you how Alexander Hamilton is from Nevis and, frankly, a huge part of our economy was the triangular trade between Europe, the eastern shore of the United States, the Caribbean.  The relationships between the United States and this part of the world have been crucial throughout our history and throughout your history.  And so we’re not writing on a blank slate as we gather here.   

I think you all know this far better than I do, that the ties between our countries are not only historical; they involve people.  When I was in Antigua last year, I was talking to somebody and I think of his siblings, two of them were in the States, and the cousins were in the States.  The personal bonds between our countries are amazing.  So many successful people in the United States, in this generation and previous generations, have come from your region.  I’m going all the way back to Alexander Hamilton, but people like Colin Powell, who ran this building 25 years ago.  I mean, our country has benefitted enormously from the ties with your region.   

And frankly, it has been a source of pain for many of us as Americans to see the United States not giving the Western Hemisphere generally the attention it deserved, and specifically the Caribbean.  The Caribbean is very much part of the Western Hemisphere.  So I’m sure you’ve all seen the stories about how the United States is, under President Trump and Secretary Rubio – we are making the Western Hemisphere a – we’re not – we are restoring – I think that’s the better word – the Western Hemisphere to its position of preeminence and priority in American foreign policy.  For far too long, we have been looking at things that are happening halfway across the world, and we have been ignoring things that are happening right in our own neighborhood.  

And so I just want to – I think it’s very important that we recognize some of the flaws of recent years in our policies and we talk together to commit to ways that we can build institutional relationships.  Because all of us in this room – I mean, we all have government positions, and it’s great, it lasts for a while.  But then all of us will be gone in a matter of years, right?  And I think the challenge for us is to create a lasting foundation that doesn’t just depend on so-and-so being friends with so-and-so.  I mean, it’s wonderful and it’s great.  One of the great things about these kinds of gatherings is that we can establish personal relationships, right?  It’s great if I can have you on WhatsApp or that kind of thing.  But that is not the basis for a lasting institutional structure of a relationship that’s going to survive over decades.   

And I think – that’s what I’m hoping that a conference like today can establish – really both those things.  I mean, again, personal ties are important in diplomacy.  But again, I think I’m looking to strengthen the structural ties, again, many of which are there.  I mean, we’re not building this from scratch, and I think we have a lot of historical precedent.  But I also want to make clear that we in the United States do not have all the answers, right?  I think I entered this job with a fair dose of humility that – I grew up in Latin America myself.  My father was a diplomat and – including in Venezuela, where actually when – during the years in the early 80s when he lived in – when we lived in Venezuela, I actually had the opportunity to visit many of your countries for the first time.  That’s when I first got the chance to go to Haiti, to Barbados, to Grenada, way back more than 40 years ago now.  And again, that only underscored for me obviously the great diversity in the Caribbean but also the importance in so many areas of the United States with these relationships in the Caribbean. 

So bringing together the leaders has been a real – your leaders – all of you has been something that’s been very important both for Secretary Rubio and for me.  I think he was delighted to go to CARICOM.  I think it was in – was it in Saint Nevis or in Saint Kitts and Nevis?  He was at a meeting or – he went recently.  And so I think he very much – again, as somebody from Florida – understands better than anybody the importance of this Caribbean region to the United States, across all dynamics, again, on a human level, on a economic level, on a security level.   

And so, again, I just want to underscore that I think this dialogue is overdue, and I just want to underscore that – I want to underscore the word “dialogue,” right?  A dialogue doesn’t mean that you have come here to have me or anybody else in the United States just give lectures, right?  I mean, I just think it’s very important that we, the United States, listen to you from the Caribbean what your vision is.  I mean, you obviously are – you all are sovereign countries; you are going to decide your fate.  And – but I think – honestly, I truly believe we wouldn’t be having this meeting if the Secretary and I didn’t believe that what is in your interests is also in our interests; that there are many, many areas where we should be deepening cooperation where there are great solutions. 

So again, I will talk today in part about further commitments the United States is going to make, and that’s fine.  I was reading through the remarks that they prepared for me here; it’s like, well, we’ll give millions of dollars for this and millions of dollars for that.  Ultimately, I’m more interested – and I think you should be more interested, or I would hope that you would be more interested – in, like, where do we get the businesses that are going to be there for the long term, that are investing in real economic opportunities that are creating a lasting foundation for the relationships?  Because ultimately, a particular grant can be fine to fill a particular need, but for a long-term growth strategy, a particular grant isn’t going to fix that.  Now, there may be particular grants that are useful insofar as they create a framework or a foundation for private-sector-led economic development.  But ultimately, I think that’s what’s going to, frankly, be the main driver here. 

So again, I just was talking to the representative of Suriname before we walked in here, and they said they had a great meeting, I think yesterday, with a private American security company that offered some services that could help them really improve their own security for their country.  I said to me, that is great.  And I feel my job, our job here at the Department of State, is to be the connective tissue between you, the leaders from your region, and the dynamic American private sector.  The American private sector is going to have more creative, cost-effective solutions for the problems you’re looking at than the U.S. Government will.  I’ll just tell you that.  I say that as somebody who works for the government right now.   

But ultimately, the greatness of the United States is not driven by the government; it’s driven by our private sector.  And so our job – or what I see our job as being is just to be an interlocutor so that our private sector is aware of the opportunities in the Caribbean, and that the Caribbean is aware of what the private sector might be interested in here.  I mean, it’s a conversation that has to go both ways. 

So let’s actually start talking a little bit about economics.  One of the things that makes me very happy is that we’re launching an investment dialogue next year precisely to bring together all of your countries with the American private sector.  And so I think – this is an issue that I also fostered out in the Pacific region.  That’s another area I’ve been very focused on, some of the island states, some of which have some similarities to some of the islands – nations of the Caribbean – not that big in terms of land mass of the country or even the population.  So they present kind of interesting economic models, where there can be opportunities for economic development, but it’s not necessarily the most obvious target as a mass export market for American companies, let’s say, but where there might be investment opportunities that you all are interested in.   

But I think for this kind of an investment conference to work, it needs a lot of advanced thought from both sides.  I think I really would urge all of your countries to think about what kind of American private sector investment you are particularly interested in in your country.  If you have an infrastructure project, a port, or a digital infrastructure project, an energy infrastructure project that you’re interested in; you want to talk to people in the telecommunications area – I mean, if you all – again, it’d be most helpful if you all let us know in advance.  If you want to see a specific company, you say, I would like to see Google, I would like to see Bechtel, I would like to see a shipping company, I’d like to see American Airlines – whatever it is, that will make this kind of a conference more helpful.  Because we don’t want to just have a conference for the sake of bringing people together to meet; we want to actually be able to have people who are actually interested in pursuing deals.  And again, we will also reach out to the private sector and say, who is interested in opportunities in the Caribbean?  And again, we will try to work it both ways. 

But again, I encourage you to really give some thought.  I don’t really have the details about what month this is yet next year, but I know it is next year.  We will keep in touch on that.  Again, that just makes me very, very happy, because ultimately, again, it’s this kind of investments that will create growth and jobs in your country and build skills. 

We also recognize that economic development entails health.  And we understand some of the health needs in your region.   

And on health, this is when I start – this is what – I’m starting to tell some of the goodies that I’m here to talk about.  I’m happy to announce we have 61 – set aside $61.5 million to launch ASPIRE, the America Strategic Partnership for Independent Regional Healthcare Excellence – that’s a long one – in order to allow the region to build its own strong, self-reliant health care workforce capacity.  So again, I think we can get more details on that, but that’s one of the deliverables that I wanted to announce to you all today.   

Second, I wanted to talk a little bit about security, and I think the assistant secretary alluded to this.  I think we have seen an uptick in recent years of drugs coming through the Caribbean from South America towards the United States.  I don’t need to tell you what a danger this is for all of us.  And frankly, as you’ve all seen if you read the news, the United States is not going to just sit by with business as usual where we have more than 100,000 Americans dying of overdose from some of these drugs just in perpetuity.  I think we’re – we have followed a approach of using the judicial system, asking for arrests, extraditions, trying people.  And I think, as you’ve seen, we now recognize that this is actually also a national security threat to our people.  We’re taking actions accordingly.  And we’d like to work with your countries to make sure that we’re all on the same page, at least in recognizing the common danger of this and seeing how we can try to address this scourge together.   

So we already have a Caribbean Basin Security Initiative, and that’s the foundation of our security partnership with 13 of the countries.  And today we are – again, my next deliverable that I’m announcing is that we’re increasing our support through CBSI, and I’m pleased to announce $37 million in new programming to protect critical digital infrastructure and strengthen port security.  Obviously, strong ports are the first line of defense.  If drugs are coming into your ports – or it’s not just drugs also; it’s also weapons and other illegal goods.  I mean, and I think in my first week in the job, the Secretary called me down to his office and handed me an article about guns going to Haiti from the Miami River and said, “Could you please deal with this?”  And that was the beginning of what has been a pretty intense involvement, as the prime minister of Haiti here, my friend, Prime Minister Fils-Aimé, knows.  I’ve been very involved in Haiti, but it really stemmed out of trying to stop the flow of guns that are going from our country into Haiti and destabilizing it.   

And I will say on this note, I am working closely with our U.S. attorney in the Southern District of Florida to make sure that our law enforcement capabilities are fully mobilized and that we are coordinating with them, so if there are issues where you think the American judicial system can actually be helpful to you as leaders in your countries who are trying to solve particular problems – if there are criminal networks that are exporting drugs from your country and you think your country may not have all the infrastructure or the legal infrastructure to address this problem, let’s work together on some of these security challenges, because our U.S. Attorney’s Office in Miami is very eager to work with you on that.   

Another big priority is illegal fishing, and I’d like to – that’s been a priority of mine worldwide.  If there are people fishing illegally in your waters, we want to work with you to address that, because obviously fish is a important resource for all of our peoples.  And I’m also – on this issue, I’m announcing an additional $55.5 million to strengthen law enforcement – I told you I had a lot of millions here to talk about – 55.5 million to strengthen law enforcement and $11 million in Foreign Military Financing to build the capabilities of your security forces.  So again, I think let’s talk about how we can work together with the security ministers, with CARICOM IMPACS, to convene the next Caribbean Basin Security Initiative security ministerial in spring 2027, next spring.   

Third – and I see I’m running low on time, but I just want to cover a range of issues that – I’m sure that all of you can flesh out what’s on your mind – trusted infrastructure is really important, and particularly secure communications networks.  Ultimately, a modern economy cannot exist without a secure network.  We all have seen vulnerabilities.  Every day you read about it in the news.  And – but without a good digital footprint, you can’t have a solid banking system, tourism system, energy grid, or government services.  And who builds those networks matters, and we would like to work with you on that.  In fact, on this – in this connection, I’m announcing $175.8 million in U.S. investment in secure infrastructure through our Caribbean and Central America underseas cables program.  This will provide trusted, high-speed connectivity across the region to build resilient, secure networks that serve your people and not outside interests.   

So together, the numbers that I have mentioned really total hundreds of millions of dollars in new commitments, but it’s not just about a certain dollar amount.  It’s about just the long term, the United States reaffirming its interest and commitment to this critical region.   

So I just want to end by underscoring the values that I think that we all share: respect for national sovereignty, the rule of law, open markets.  These are some of the central tenets that underlie our relationships.  And these are – by focusing on these core issues, that’s how we’re going to stimulate economic growth, attract investment, and allow you and us to provide prosperity and security for our – your citizens and our citizens.  So again, as somebody who is very, very committed to your region, I just say that there are few events that I have attended during my time as Deputy Secretary of State that I’m as excited to be part of as this one.   

I will close by just saying my last class in college, at Harvard College, was Sociology 113 that was taught by Orlando Patterson.  He was visiting at Harvard that year.  And it was on the sociology of the Caribbean, just all the many fascinating aspects of culture that emerged in your region.  I mean, you have such an interesting mixture, just looking at the backgrounds of your countries.  And I remember my last exam in college was comparing Rastafarianism in Jamaica with Vodou in Haiti and how some of those ancestral beliefs affected the modern development of those countries. 

And I just want to say that, at least in me, I want you to know that you have a true friend of the Caribbean, someone who, again, is very cognizant of the critical role that your region has always played in the development of our country, and I think it is – you’re part of our past, you’re part of our present, and part of our future, and vice versa, I think.  And I just want to, on that note, say how pleased and excited I am to welcome all of you here.  And I hope this is a very enriching experience for all of you, as I’m sure it will be for us.  Thank you very much.  (Applause.) 

MS WALKE:  Thank you.  And may I now ask Prime Minister Pierre of Saint Lucia, our CARICOM chair, to please come to the podium to deliver your remarks?  Thank you.  (Applause.)   

PRIME MINISTER PIERRE:  Thank you very much.  Good morning, everyone.  Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau, Assistant Secretary Juan Pablo, fellow heads of government, heads of delegation, ladies and gentlemen, I’ve been told I have three minutes.  (Laughter.) 

DEPUTY SECRETARY LANDAU:  I’m sorry.  I went way over on mine, so —  

PRIME MINISTER PIERRE:  I shall remain within my three minutes.  Good morning, everyone.  I speak as Prime Minister of Saint Lucia and chairman of the Caribbean Community.  I thank the Government of the United States for convening this dialogue and for its hospitality.  This meeting responds to the call by CARICOM leaders for political-level consultations following our constructive engagement with Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Saint Kitts and Nevis in February.   

We value this relationship.  Our countries are connected by geography, commerce, tourism, family, and friendship.  The Caribbean community is a close neighbor, a stable democratic partner, and a region open to investment.  We seek a more strategic partnership sustained by regular dialogue and measured by improvements in the daily lives of our people.   

For Caribbean families, energy security means affordable electricity.  Economic cooperation means jobs, investment, and opportunity.  Security cooperation means safer communities.  Disaster preparedness means knowing that help will arrive when it is needed and will arrive promptly.  These are shared interests. 

Our discussions today should translate into practical commitments financing for resilient energy systems, predictable trade and stronger commercial partnerships, secure infrastructure, stronger health systems and disaster response, and coordinated action against organized crime and illicit firearms trafficking.  Haiti must remain central to our attention.  We appreciate the U.S.’s role and welcome the extension of the United Nations mandate for the Gang Suppression Force.  CARICOM continues – continues its work through the Eminent Persons Group.  Sustained international assistance and credible elections with the widest possible participation are essential to restoring confidence and supporting Haiti’s return to stability. 

Our dialogue must also make room for immigration and migration matters, with profound implications for our communities and our people-to-people ties.  The strength of today’s meeting will be demonstrated by what follows it.  Let us connect political dialogue with sustained technical engagements, identify priorities, and establish clear arrangements for follow-up between governments and the private sector.  The CARICOM Secretariat will help coordinate the community’s technical work alongside our national authorities and regional institutions.  CARICOM comes to this table ready to listen, ready to engage, and ready to build a partnership that delivers mutual benefit, with respect for our sovereignty and our shared aspirations. 

I look forward to these discussions and the (inaudible) development of the people of the region.  I thank you.  (Applause.)

item.title: Sanctioning Cuban State-Owned Banco Internacional de Comercio, S.A. (BICSA)
item.dc:creator: Marco Rubio, Secretary of State
item.description:
Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

Sanctioning Cuban State-Owned Banco Internacional de Comercio, S.A. (BICSA)

Press Statement

October 15, 2026

President Trump has been absolutely clear:  under his administration, the United States will not tolerate terrorism, organized crime or extra-hemispheric forces spreading anti-American influence in our region.  For too long, Communist Cuba has been allowed to operate as an outpost for malign actors and terror groups – including the Islamic Republic of Iran, the world’s number one state sponsor of terrorism – to target the United States.

Cuba’s BANCO INTERNACIONAL DE COMERCIO S.A. (BICSA) has provided services to the designated Iran’s Karafarin Bank since at least 2022.  The Department of the Treasury sanctioned Karafarin Bank pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 13902 in 2020.  Today, in concert with a Department of the Treasury action on Iranian financial actors, I am sanctioning the Cuban state-owned BICSA pursuant to Section 2(a)(i)(A) of E.O. 14404 for operating in or having operated in the financial services sector of the Cuban economy.

Let me be clear:  the Trump Administration will not tolerate a rogue state hosting hostile foreign military, intelligence and terror operations less than a hundred miles from the American homeland.  We will continue to aggressively identify and eliminate the Cuban regime’s financial and security interconnections with Iran and other dangerous and hostile states and actors.

The Department’s actions are being taken pursuant to E.O. 14404, which authorizes sweeping sanctions on Cuba, including against persons who support the Cuban regime’s security apparatus and those responsible for repression in Cuba and other threats to U.S. national security.  These actions also further both E.O. 14380, “Addressing Threats to the United States by the Government of Cuba” and National Security Presidential Memorandum 5, which directs the Executive Branch to improve human rights, encourage the rule of law, foster free markets and free enterprise, and promote democracy in Cuba.

Sanctions Implications 

As a result of today’s sanctions actions, and in accordance with E.O. 14404 of May 1, 2026, “Imposing Sanctions on Those Responsible for Repression in Cuba and for Threats to U.S. National Security and Foreign Policy,” all property and interests in property of the designated person described above that are in the United States or in possession or control of U.S. persons are blocked and must be reported to the Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC).  Additionally, all entities that are owned individually or in the aggregate, 50 percent or more by one or more blocked persons are also blocked.

Any transaction or dealing by U.S. persons or persons subject to the jurisdiction of the United States in property or interests of designated or otherwise blocked persons are prohibited unless authorized or exempt.  These prohibitions include the making of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services by, to, or for the benefit of any blocked person and the receipt of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services from any such person.  Foreign persons that engage in transactions with persons designated pursuant to E.O. 14404—or that operate or have operated in the energy, defense and related materiel, metals and mining, financial services, or security sector of the Cuban economy, as identified in E.O. 14404—are themselves at risk of sanctions.  Non-U.S. persons, including foreign financial institutions, should proceed with caution in any dealings with a party sanctioned under this authority.  Actions to return assets to a sanctioned party or transfer them to another jurisdiction for potential use by the target expose non-U.S. persons to significant sanctions risk.  All property and interests in property of persons that are blocked pursuant to the Cuban Assets Control Regulations (CACR) are blocked.  The CACR prohibits persons subject to U.S. jurisdiction from dealing in property in which Cuba or a Cuban national has an interest, unless authorized or exempt.

The power and integrity of U.S. government sanctions derive not only from the U.S. government’s ability to designate and add persons to the List of Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons (SDN List), but also from its willingness to remove persons from the SDN List consistent with the law.  The ultimate goal of sanctions is not to punish, but to bring about a positive change in behavior.

Petitions for removal from the SDN List may be routed through OFAC’s Reconsiderations Portal.  Petitioners may also refer to the Department of State’s Delisting Guidance page.

item.title: Secretary Rubio’s Call with Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy
item.dc:creator: Office of the Spokesman
item.description:
Office of the Spokesman

Secretary Rubio’s Call with Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy

Readout

October 14, 2026

Secretary of State Marco Rubio spoke today with Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed Ali. The Secretary and Prime Minister discussed heightened tensions with Eritrea.

The Secretary supports de-escalation by all sides. The only sustainable solution to internal and external tensions is achieved through dialogue and engagement as agreed to in the 2018 Ethiopia-Eritrea peace framework.

The Secretary stressed that all countries in the Horn of Africa must respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of their neighbors and avoid cross-border incursions. The Secretary emphasized that the region cannot tolerate more conflict.

Secretary Rubio’s Call with Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy

Readout

October 14, 2026

Secretary of State Marco Rubio spoke today with Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed Ali. The Secretary and Prime Minister discussed heightened tensions with Eritrea.

The Secretary supports de-escalation by all sides. The only sustainable solution to internal and external tensions is achieved through dialogue and engagement as agreed to in the 2018 Ethiopia-Eritrea peace framework.

The Secretary stressed that all countries in the Horn of Africa must respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of their neighbors and avoid cross-border incursions. The Secretary emphasized that the region cannot tolerate more conflict.
